purpose: The naming contract, written once and executed twice. tests/naming.test.ts runs these through the server resolver; tests/naming-parity.test.ts runs the same rows through the web client's mirror. A rule that lives in one implementation and not the other cannot survive both files.

cases.name: an operator alias outranks a manifest, an authored name, a directory and a task
cases.claim: A human who renamed a session gets the name they chose, whatever the machine thinks it knows.

cases.name: a workspace alias names the session when no agent alias exists
cases.claim: The operator labelled the pane and nothing else; that is still a human naming this session.

cases.name: an agent alias outranks a workspace alias
cases.claim: A workspace label names a cmux pane and sibling panes share one, so the agent-specific label is the more precise intent.

cases.name: a whitespace-only alias is not an alias
cases.claim: An operator who cleared the rename box did not name the session; the chain must carry on past it.

cases.name: a manifest lane name outranks an authored name, a directory and a task
cases.claim: The run declaration names the lane before it starts, so provider titles and filesystem guesses cannot replace that stable identity.

cases.name: a manifest names its orchestrator after the run rather than a lane
cases.claim: The orchestrator owns the declared run, so its stable name is the run id while workers use their lane ids.

cases.name: a manifest verifier lane uses its lane id
cases.claim: Non-orchestrator declared roles share the lane-id naming rule; the role does not become the name.

cases.name: a manifest tester lane uses its lane id
cases.claim: A declared tester is still a lane in the run, so the lane id is the stable board name.

cases.name: a manifest monitor lane uses its lane id
cases.claim: Monitor is a first-class declared role and still names from the lane, not from the role word.

cases.name: a manifest automation lane uses its lane id
cases.claim: Automation lanes are declared the same way as workers — the run's lane id is the name.

cases.name: a manifest human lane uses its lane id
cases.claim: A human seat declared in the run is still a lane; the operator's alias tier is what overrides it, not the role itself.

cases.name: an authored name outranks the directory it happens to run in
cases.claim: This is the flip. Today 'Lifecycle Mapper' loses to 'Claude · the-mountain-main' because the client cannot tell an authored name from a guessed one, so the folder wins and 360 sessions share a name.

cases.name: an authored name outranks a task line
cases.claim: The task says what the agent was asked to do; the authored name says what it is called.

evidence.taskName: Harden the forecast service bearer auth

cases.name: a launcher-supplied environment name is an authored name
cases.claim: Claude root sessions pass no explicit name anywhere else, so ANT_HILL_AGENT_NAME is their only authored path.

cases.name: a later task outranks a stale launch-env name
cases.claim: authoredBy launch-env is leftover from launch or the first naming pass. A resumed pane's current task is the work happening now, so that leftover must not keep the name.

cases.name: Cursor's untitled-composer placeholder is not an authored name
cases.claim: 'new agent' is Cursor's own boilerplate for a composer nobody has titled. Accepting it would give every untitled Cursor session the same authored name.

cases.name: an OMP status row is not an authored name
cases.claim: 'Session update' is periodic boilerplate that arrives in a name-shaped field.

cases.name: the directory a session began in names it, not the one it wandered to
cases.claim: Freezing at origin is the whole point: this session recorded six cwd changes in four minutes and was published under another lane's name.

cases.name: a session started in the home directory is named Home, not after the operator
cases.claim: The basename of $HOME is a username; naming every session after the operator tells nobody anything.

cases.name: a trailing slash does not make a different directory
cases.claim: Two spellings of one path must not produce two names, or the freeze is worthless.

cases.name: the origin directory outranks the task line
cases.claim: A prompt blob is not a name. The board learned this the hard way when prompts became terminal titles operators had to hunt through.

cases.name: the task line names a session that recorded no directory
cases.claim: Last thing left that carries meaning.

cases.name: an attachment header is not a task name
cases.claim: A transcript whose first content is a file attachment has told us nothing about what the agent is.

cases.name: a session with no evidence at all still gets its provider's name
cases.claim: Never blank. A row with no name is a row an operator cannot refer to.

cases.name: a name of exactly the operator cap is left alone
cases.claim: 80 characters is what program-aliases.ts already accepts by hand, so it must survive here untouched.

cases.claim: A derived name an operator is forbidden to retype by hand is a name they cannot search for.

fleets.name: two sessions in one worktree stop sharing a name
fleets.claim: The live board's headline failure: 360 sessions named 'Claude · the-mountain-main'. The base survives so the name still reads; the tail of the session id separates them.

fleets.name: a name nobody else has is left alone
fleets.claim: A tag on every row would be noise on a board where most names should end up distinct once operators and launchers name things.

fleets.name: three sessions sharing a name all get separated, and a fourth is untouched
fleets.claim: Disambiguation is per name, not per board: one crowded folder must not put a tag on an unrelated row.

fleets.name: a disambiguator that is itself shared escalates to the whole session id
fleets.claim: A tag that settles nothing is worse than no tag, because it looks like it settled something. Acceptance turns on no two sessions sharing a name.

fleets.name: an operator alias survives disambiguation untagged when it is already unique
fleets.claim: Naming a session by hand is the operator's escape hatch out of a crowded folder, and it has to actually work.

fleets.name: a sticky tag survives when a third collision joins later
fleets.claim: Once a session has been tagged, a later peer must not rewrite that tag — stickiness is write-once per agent id, not recomputed from the current fleet.
